decisions.reason: SOL keeps the repeated breath-holding while making the account unfold naturally.
SOL keeps the news’s unusual weight and makes the narrator’s prior expectation clear.
SOL keeps the numbers’ contribution to the weight of the news.
The terminology veto applies: BASE retains the established title Son of Heaven; SOL replaces it with an ambiguous pronoun.
SOL keeps the contrast between his youthful age and aged appearance, with no change in the deathbed meaning.
SOL keeps both descriptions of the technique; the omitted transition adds no distinct meaning.
The source says the technique was no better than a poisoned grail; SOL turns that comparison into a direct description.
“Alive and well” naturally preserves the source’s image of the values still living in that age.
SOL keeps the one blood relative’s future burden and the emphasis on protecting them.
SOL keeps the sense that the Son of Heaven also has someone to protect.
The protected-term veto applies: BASE uses the established rendering Third Rate; SOL changes its capitalization and form.
SOL preserves the galloping hooves shaking the earth without adding a separate sound image.
SOL keeps both groups’ shame and self-blame.
SOL keeps the point that the motives of those taking up arms did not matter.
The punctuation change does not alter the stern expression or his reaction.
SOL preserves the quiet addition and correctly lets the following dialogue continue the sentence.
BASE’s “as though they meant it” changes the resolve, while SOL’s “resolve that took” is awkward and misses the sense of fighting to match their resolve.
decisions.replacement: “They chose their path. They’d already accepted that they might die, and they fought with courage to match. More bravely than anyone.”

decisions.reason: Dropping “And” keeps the meaning and makes the continuation less stiff.
SOL makes explicit that the next name is also connected to Asmodeus, as the surrounding passage indicates.
SOL keeps the contrasting weather and the storm’s world-swallowing force.
SOL keeps the sight beyond the sun-raised heat haze without changing what appears.
“Sounded their deep call” keeps the drums’ deep resonance without the overly formal “toll.”
SOL follows the source’s east-west-south-north order.
SOL keeps the banners surging in from the hills, plains, and Yellow River.
The reordered clause keeps the same room-reading joke and informal voice.
“Do you not hear me?” naturally preserves the demand to prepare for battle.
BASE’s “the Great Sir” is more idiomatic for the established form of address; SOL’s bare title reads awkwardly here.
SOL keeps Jeok Cheongang’s exasperation and the qi-deviation complaint.
SOL keeps the Hong Gil-dong comparison and the contrast with plain old Gil-dung.
SOL keeps the crude road-side pile image and the crowd edging around him.
BASE’s “the Great Sir” is more idiomatic for this established form of address; SOL’s bare title reads awkwardly.
SOL keeps the commoners’ suspiciously detailed knowledge of martial-arts clichés.
BASE preserves the source’s timing that the cheer swallowed the murmurs in an instant.
SOL keeps the distant wind catching and billowing the banners without implying it carried the roar.
SOL keeps the unfamiliar-name point without misrendering Korean 글자 as “words.”
SOL keeps the two banners’ size and height; the omitted “And” adds no meaning.
“Presence” keeps the focus on the man’s arrival and preserves the onlookers’ astonishment.
SOL keeps the golden dragon visible through the haze and the people’s response.
“Uproar” preserves the source’s repeated sense of commotion.
SOL keeps Jeok Cheongang’s observation that the whole place has erupted into disorder.
“Until they bled” keeps the injury without changing the physical action.
BASE keeps the focus on how close the people are to seeing the Emperor’s face; SOL shifts it to making out the procession.
SOL naturally conveys the North Korean three-Kim reference instead of the misleading “three-generation ruling family.”
“Look around” naturally preserves Jeok Cheongang’s caution to mind the many listeners.
SOL adds that Jeok Cheongang watched the procession here and loses the source’s quick turn; BASE preserves the action and timing.
BASE keeps the procession drawing nearer as Jeok Cheongang watches; SOL drops that action from this sentence.
“Ah” better preserves the exasperated interjection than BASE’s added “God.”
SOL preserves the nostril-flaring detail and the narrator’s suppressed snicker.
SOL keeps the rumbling sound effect.
BASE keeps joy and tears together beneath the cheers; SOL moves the tears into the people’s voices.
SOL preserves the fans-and-haters setup and the narrator’s correction to common people.
Dropping “that” leaves the desert reference and contrast intact.
SOL keeps the Emperor’s gentle smile toward the narrator, who is standing stiffly upright.
